newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo 1997 steel production seen at 1.2 mln tonnes.
newsitem.headline: Yugo 1997 steel production seen at 1.2 mln tonnes.

text.p: Yugoslavia's 1997 steel output is set to reach 1.2 million tonnes, returning to its 1989 level, the head of the Yugoslav Iron and Steel Federation said on Monday.

"We expect to maintain the strong upward trend from the last quarter of this year and increase capacity utilisation in 1997, so that the total production reaches 1.2 million tonnes," Arsenije Jovanovic told Reuters.
Yugoslav steelworks produced 611,000 tonnes of steel from January to November 1996, up on 169,304 tonnes over the same period 1995, the federation said in its latest monthly report.
"Capacity utilisation ran around 50 percent," Jovanovic said, adding that it was expected to start rising during the second half of 1997.
The largest Yugoslav steelworks of Smederevo produced 498,136 tonnes of steel over the period, while the Niksic steel factory produced 112,864 tonnes, the report said.
"We can be satisfied with 1996 results, because the ferrous metallurgy was one of the branches recovering faster than the rest of the industry," Jovanovic said.

But despite production growing 3.6 times over 1995, Yugoslav steelers have not solved their key problems of reduced home market, slow revival of domestic industries and alarmingly high imports from Eastern and Central Europe.
The value of steel imports totalled $139 million for the January-November period and accounted for 41.4 percent of domestic consumption.

Facing bitter competition from eastern European suppliers, Yugoslav steelmakers appealed to the government twice this year to protect the industry. Yugoslav steelmakers charge that eastern European suppliers deliver goods at dumping prices,
The issue is expected to be addressed again in January, when steel producers plan to meet government officials. In the meantime, import quotas remain the only protection.

"But we seek more efficient protection. We want any dumping to be called by its name and we insist on standard quality of those products. We want a cultivated and orderly market, with efficient protection and fair competition," Jovanovic said.
